questions.q: Who is Nagarjun (नागार्जुन) and what is his primary literary identity? (Answer in 2-3 sentences.)
questions.a: Nagarjun (1929–1990) was a prominent Hindi poet, novelist, and journalist associated with the Progressive Writers' Movement (प्रगतिशील लेखक आंदोलन). He wrote in Khari Boli, Maithili, and Sanskrit, and is known for giving voice to the marginalized — peasants, laborers, and street performers — using simple, earthy language. A wrong answer (e.g., "He was a classical Sanskrit poet") reveals the student lacks awareness of his modern, socially engaged identity and may confuse him with ancient poets.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why knowing the socio-political context of a poem is essential before analyzing its literary devices.
questions.a: Literary devices serve the poet's message; without context, a metaphor might seem decorative rather than a tool for social critique. For Nagarjun, the 'street performer' is not just a character but a symbol of exploited labor. A wrong answer (e.g., "Context is only for history class") shows the student treats literature as isolated from society, a misconception that leads to superficial board answers.

questions.q: The textbook mentions Nagarjun wrote in "Hkk"kk" (Khari Boli) as well as Maithili and Sanskrit. Apply this: How does his choice of Khari Boli (modern standard Hindi) instead of highly Sanskritized Hindi affect the poem's reach and impact?
questions.a: Khari Boli was the language of common people in North India; using it made his poetry accessible to the very masses he wrote about — peasants, workers, street performers. It also aligned with the Progressive Writers' goal of literature for social change. A wrong answer (e.g., "It makes the poem harder to understand") misses the democratic intent and shows ignorance of the language politics of the time.

questions.q: Compare the background note on Nagarjun with what you know about Premchand (from Class 11). How do their journalistic backgrounds influence their literary focus?
questions.a: Both worked as journalists — Premchand edited 'Hans', Nagarjun worked for 'Navlekhan' and other papers. Journalism trained them to observe ground realities, report on exploitation, and write with urgency. This shows in their focus on rural poverty, feudalism, and the dignity of labor. A wrong answer (e.g., "Journalism has no effect on fiction") fails to see the crossover between reportage and creative writing, a key concept in Indian literary history.

questions.q: Evaluate: The background note says Nagarjun's poetry "does not only take up big issues but also makes the ignored nuances of society its subject." Defend or challenge this statement using one example from any Nagarjun poem you have read earlier (or from the note itself).
questions.a: Defend: His poem 'जकेनकल' (mentioned in the note) takes a seemingly small episode — a peasant's struggle — and reveals the entire feudal structure. The note itself says he gave literary status to 'ignored nuances' like a street performer's life. A wrong answer (e.g., "He only writes about big revolutions") shows the student hasn't grasped the 'micro-macro' link central to progressive literature.

questions.q: Create a 4-line stanza in simple Hindi (Khari Boli) that introduces a marginalized worker (e.g., a ragpicker, a construction laborer) in the style of Nagarjun — using direct address and concrete imagery.
questions.a: A good answer will use everyday words (e.g., "कूड़ा बीनने वाला", "ईंट ढोने वाला"), address the worker directly ("तू"), and show a specific physical detail ("हाथों में छाले", "पसीने की गंध"). A poor answer uses abstract language ("गरीब", "शोषण") or Sanskritized vocabulary, missing Nagarjun's hallmark of concrete, spoken-language immediacy.
